paragraphs.text: In the times of the holy apostles, when the divinity of the Word and his dispensation in the flesh were being proclaimed through them to mankind, the herald and apostle of the whole world, passing through the nations, came to certain parts of Isauria, as the houses of prayer there show that he visited them. When he learned that all their cities and the surrounding countryside were more madly given than any other nation to the deceit of idols and to their foul sacrifices, he was eager to go up into the eastern parts as well. But he was prevented by the Spirit because of their great unbelief and savagery. Knowing that they would not receive the preaching, he turned away from them because of the Lord's saying, "Do not throw your pearls before swine," and judged it necessary to preach the word first, without hindrance, to others who were waiting for it, in accordance with the revelation of the Spirit.

The whole adjoining Taurus range was crowded with populous villages set on wooded mountains, and there were tyrants and independent chieftains there. Having taken on from their surroundings a rather savage character, these people were not easily persuaded to come to the mystery of godliness, and so the preaching of the gospel to them was put off at that time. For their lawless and demonic madness for idols prevailed for a long time.

After a very long time, a certain Nestor was found in those parts, a good root. He had a wife named Nadan, and they lived in a village called Bidana, about eighteen stades from the city of Isaura. They brought forth a fruit of godliness, whom they named Conon.

When he had come of age, his parents betrothed him to a girl named Anna. But when the time of the wedding arrived, the archangel Michael appeared to Conon in shining clothing, and conversing with him he instructed him in the truths of the mystery. Conon was pierced to the heart and at once gave his heart over to it, and he asked for baptism. He made his request as though to a man, for he thought the archangel was a human being. The archangel, seeing that Conon had been pierced to the heart, had eagerly received the word and was seeking baptism, led him to some water, brought him down into it and baptized him in the holy and blessed threefold name. He gave him a pearl, sealed him and sanctified him, and then withdrew from his sight; but he remained with him invisibly, since Conon had been sanctified and filled with the Holy Spirit.

His parents, not knowing about this, carried through the marriage contract, and he brought home his betrothed and she came to live with him. But instead of the expected wedding bed, at the very outset he took a lighted lamp, put it under a bushel, and said to his wife, who was a virgin, "Which is sweeter, light or darkness?" When she agreed that light was sweeter, he set before her words of counsel drawn from the divine grace given him by the Holy Spirit and changed the girl's mind. They remained undefiled and practiced a strict ascetic life in all purity, keeping their bodies uncorrupted. When the righteous man's mother learned of this, she gave her assent to their resolve with praise, and she too persevered in their way of life.

Not long afterward, through the grace of the archangel, he converted his own father as well and made him well-pleasing to God. His father also completed martyrdom for Christ, as his house of prayer on the spot, in the middle of the village of Bidana, testifies. When the wife of Saint Conon died uncorrupted, and his mother likewise, he laid them in a single tomb. He remained alone by himself, day by day increasing, in all endurance, courage and ascetic discipline, the treasure given him by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and guarding it out of sight until the time when he was to be revealed.

The birthday feast of Apollo was being held in a most dreadful cave called Kaklimi, which ran far underground and was dark. There the inhabitants of Isauropolis and the surrounding countryside were accustomed to celebrate the festival, and many tens of thousands of Isaurian men and women flocked to it. (The place lies in wild and impassable mountains, four miles from the city.) On that day, then, as the crowds were gathering and about to set out from the city, Saint Conon suddenly appeared before them in the city itself, by now advanced in years. Seeing them armed and ready to rush off to the impiety before them, he cried out to them in their own language, "Men, stop, and I will ask you a question." And they stopped.
He said to them, "What is this battle array for, and why are you in such a hurry? Is some necessity of war calling you?" They said, "No, we are offering a sacrifice to the god Apollo."

The saint said to them, "And who is this Apollo? I want to learn. What is his power, or what does he do?" They told him, "He arms us and makes us strong in war, as he did our fathers too; for they handed this custom down to us." They said this because they were the bravest allies of the Romans, as the account below shows more fully from the inscriptions carved in the city.
Saint Conon asked them mockingly, "Have you, then, heard a voice from him, or has he ever uttered a sound to anyone?" They said, "No, but the custom of our fathers assures us."

He said to them, "But your fathers went astray like dumb beasts, because they had no knowledge of the true God. If they had known him, they would not have shown such zeal for a deaf and motionless stone. Give me leave to deal with him, and I will show you what it is you worship and call your god. I will smear him with soot and see whether he can wash himself clean. Or give me an iron hammer and I will smash him, and see whether he can restore himself to his shape. I will offer him food and see whether he stretches out a hand, takes it and eats.

"How long will you be foolish and fail to understand these things? But now listen to me, for I too am of your race, though a stranger to your practices. Abstain from these things, and I will teach you what God you ought to worship and adore: the God who sits in the highest, who is mighty and invisible yet sees all things, the Creator of heaven and earth and sea and all that is in them. He is a strong and mighty king, who saves his own in war and wars down his enemies and those who sacrifice to idols. Those who say that carved or molten images are gods he wars down as rebels. And to those who sacrifice to demons and not to God he is a relentless enemy. He does not seek sacrifices of blood, but wants to be known without error and believed by those who come to him.

"One must believe in him simply and without guile, that he is the true God and the Father of an only-begotten Son, who is true God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is inseparable from the Father and through whom he also made the ages. Sharing in the Godhead and the kingdom, and with the Son, is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, beneficent and life-giving, who is over all his works. This threefold name, then, is one Godhead; God is one.

"He is jealous and a fire that consumes his enemies: those who worship idols as gods and sacrifice on the altars of demons he punishes and burns up on the day of wrath and vengeance. But he is good beyond measure to all who call upon him and believe in him, especially when they turn to him from impiety. He loves those who love him and glorifies those who glorify him. He rejoices in peace and in love for one another. He delights, too, in purity and self-control, in a dignified life and in humility. So if you do not love him who hates evil and rejoices in good, it is quite plain that you are wicked men and rebels, and you will never be able to withstand him when he is angry.

"So listen, and do not stiffen your necks against him, for, as I said, you will never be able to withstand the wrath of his anger; against such people he is relentless in his wrath. Abandon and abstain from what you are now doing in service of the devil who deceives you, and turn to our Lord Jesus Christ, and he will fill you with all his good things."

But as he urged them to abstain from such folly and turn to what brings salvation, they—barbarians, if one must call them that, and wholly irrational—thought the holy man was speaking to them in a foreign tongue, and they remained disobedient to him. They even turned in anger against him, because he was hindering their customary feast, or rather was overturning it.

An uproar broke out among them. Some rushed to kill him, while others held back their onslaught and stopped them, since they had very nearly listened to him gladly and wanted to change their ways, though they were not yet fully convinced. When the first group had at last given up the attempt, those who seemed inclined to change began to say to the righteous man, "How can you convince us that there is a God greater than the one we worship?"

He talked with them and admonished them at length, but they were not moved at all; rather, they disbelieved all the more, until at last they came to testing him by demanding miracles, saying to him, "What can the God you worship do, so that we may believe in him? Show us even one sign, and we will believe in him and in you."

When Saint Conon saw their great unbelief and that they were demanding a sign from him, he said to them, "Bear with me a little, and let us do this. Are there not among you some in the prime of youth and swift of foot, many others past their prime, and still others on horseback? Let us all race together to the place where you customarily hold your festival. You go on ahead, and I, being an old man, will follow; and let us give each other our word: whoever gets ahead and reaches the place first shall win the verdict of victory, as one whose God is mighty; but the god of the one who arrives last shall suffer the penalty of defeat, as being no god."

Since there was no contest in what he proposed, they laughed at him and agreed, relying on the speed of their horses and the nimbleness of their legs. For they said to one another, "He will not be able to reach the place even after four days. How can he hold out on so long a road, especially one so hard to travel?"

Saint Conon, the man of God, understanding that they had written him off as unable to fulfill these terms, became all the more eager, and praying privately he said, "Master and Lord, God the Father almighty, and Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world came to be, mighty God, grant the power of your Holy Spirit. Strengthen me, and bind this whole multitude, so that they may learn that they are in error in what they worship; and hobble them, so that they may know that you are God and there is no other besides you. And may the holy archangel Michael help me as well, who brought me to the knowledge of you and made your mystery known to me from my youth."

At once Saint Michael stood beside him. He strengthened the saint and brought him safely to the place without fatigue, but he enclosed the barbarians in blindness as they began their journey. They went round in circles and wandered about in the mountains, tumbling into hollows among the cliffs, and they spent the whole day and that night this way, until they had no strength left, nor a sound body or bone, and could not pass from one spot to another. Saint Conon, having arrived first, waited for them as agreed. When he saw that they were late, he got up early the next day, went back, and found them in the place where he had left them.

Seeing him suddenly, they were struck with amazement. He came up to them and fell upon them with reproaches, saying, "Why have you done this, leaving me waiting for you until now, so that I was forced to come back to you again?" They, stricken through and with no life left in them, told him what had happened and begged him to set them on the road. He agreed and prayed, and through the archangel he removed their blindness; and then, having come to themselves, they followed him.

When they arrived at the place, the saint said to them, "You have been convinced. Now then, act according to our proposal and agreement. For see, you have been defeated, you and your god. So hand him over to me, and I will punish your god."

But they persisted shamelessly in their unbelief and said, "You shall not lay the blame on our god. We are the ones to blame, who lost our way on the road; he was not defeated." And they overbore him by force, without fulfilling what they had agreed.

So he said to them again, "What do you want, then: to believe in my God or in the one you worship?" They said, "We must believe in the one we worship." He said to them, "And whatever this falsely named god says, will you obey him?"

They all shouted that they would abide by it. When they had given him their pledge on this, the saint, kindled in spirit, ran to the statue. The statue stood on a high place, and he rebuked it sternly and said to it, "I say to you, Jesus Christ my God commands you to come down." Shaking with fear at the command, the idol fell from its place, came rolling up beside the saint, and stood upright. Everyone shuddered with fear, astounded at the miracle, and cried out loudly.

He motioned to them with his hand and said to them, "Are you convinced now at least, or not yet?" For he saw some of them grumbling. Some agreed, but others refused to believe, as though the miracle were not a great one.

But he did not give way to them; he kept on exhorting them, saying, "Oh, what great folly is yours! How long will you persist in your madness? The God who is does not want those who belong to him and worship him to be like this, but to have hearts like his own. Being true, he wants his own to be true; being good, he wants his own to be good; being just, he wishes his own to be like him. In short, he wants his own to be such as he himself is. Such, then, is my God. But yours, being made of stone, has turned your hearts to stone; being a deceiver and a devil, he wants to lead you astray; and being faithless, he makes you faithless. So do not persist in these things, but listen to me and abstain from the madness of idols and the error they bring, for they are not gods; the one I am telling you of is God. Do you want to hear from this stone that you worship that you are in error? Come close to me and listen."

They drew near and watched him intently, to see something more of what he was doing. Saint Conon, with great menace, rebuked the idol standing there sternly and said, "Tell me, you: who is God? You, or the one I preach?"

Then, in great fear, their stone god stretched out its hands to heaven and spoke in a human voice, saying, "There is one God, one Christ, the one whom you proclaim." When this miracle had taken place, the whole crowd of those tens of thousands raised a great shout, saying, "One is the God of Conon! The God of Conon has conquered!"

To this day the whole of Isauria and its surrounding region gather and shout these words on the glorious day of the commemoration of Saint Conon, coming out of their houses with torches in the evening and going to his house of prayer for the vigil, in the village called Bidana.

As they kept on shouting at the extraordinary miracle, he motioned to them with his hand and with difficulty quieted them, saying, "Now at least do you admit the defeat of your god? Hand him over, then, and I will punish him." Many of the crowd believed, rushed forward and smashed the statue, and were baptized.

But the rest still refused to believe, through the working of the devil, and were vexed at the smashing of their image, and they devised another scheme: to set the power of an evil demon against the holy man. This demon dwelt in an inaccessible cave and seemed to them a fearsome thing, being hostile and destructive to them; they served it with sacrifices, not so that it would help them but so that it would not harm them. The believers too begged him on this matter to consent to drive out that evil spirit, since it had maimed many, and to go with them to that place; the others were testing him, thinking he would not dare, or would not overcome the evil one. Saint Conon, persuaded by them, went eagerly with them to the place.

The whole crowd came, and lighting torches they went down into that rocky chasm, full of fear and apprehension. Seeing them in such a state, he cried out, "Do not be afraid; for now you will see its end." Standing at the bottom of its lair, he rebuked that unclean spirit, commanding it to show itself plainly to all. From within it cried out, uttering pleas not to have its hideous form exposed. When he rebuked it sternly, it came out of a hole in great fear, rolling along as if floating, and appeared to everyone like an old woman whose body was shriveled and ravaged by disease. The whole crowd cried out, shouting the same words as before: "One is the God of Conon! The God of Conon has conquered!" And he threatened that evil spirit and charged it never to appear anywhere again nor to harm anyone.

Then Saint Conon groaned over them, saying and showing them, "Who is it that lords it over you? See what kind of things you worship: lifeless, voiceless and motionless, worked by these destructive and unclean spirits to lead you astray to your ruin, not of your bodies only but of your souls as well. How long, then, will you go on hardening your souls like this? Come to your senses at last from the error of idols and turn to the living God, to the true God, the only-begotten Son, the Lord Jesus Christ. Consider only this: how great is his goodness, that he has been patient with you. Though he ought to have destroyed you too for your great unbelief, he did not do so, but spared you. He has done these wonders so that, convinced that his name can do all things, you may turn to him and be saved. Let the time of ignorance that is past be enough for you. So now that you have come to know him, worship him, and he will forgive you what has gone before."

Most of the crowd believed and worshiped God, and having come to know him they were persuaded to be baptized, rejoicing in the mystery of Christ. As they returned, the saint led them in singing psalms, and they answered him in the responses; and so they went up to the city, following him and glorifying the Lord Jesus Christ.

After this they spent a long time with him and were instructed by him, being strengthened by the Holy Spirit. From then until today the whole of Isauropolis and its surrounding region have continued in faith in the Lord, growing and multiplying day by day through saving baptism. Many other healings and miracles were also performed by Saint Conon, and they rejoiced in him and in the miracles he performed.

After this it happened that some of the distinguished and notable men of the city suffered a robbery and lost a great deal of money, gold and silver and other property. Many people of the city were seized on suspicion and imprisoned and were about to be put in danger though innocent. Being at a loss for any evidence to trace the stolen goods, the victims ran to the blessed Conon in supplication and told him what had happened. Moreover, the relatives and friends of those who had been brought into this trouble on suspicion also fell at the saint's feet, pleading with him.

Seeing the distress of those who had been robbed and of those held without cause, he hurried up to the city with them. Standing in the middle of the city before everyone, he stretched out his hands to heaven and earnestly called on his own Master, Jesus Christ, to reveal the matter to him, because of the danger to so many. And by the grace of the Holy Spirit it was revealed to him where the stolen goods were. He gave thanks to God and said to them, "Follow me." And they followed him.

After they had gone a long way, the place was shown to him by the archangel Michael on one of the mountains, where everything they were looking for lay hidden under a rock. They took it all up and brought it into the city, and setting it down in the open, they cried out in astonishment, showing the stolen goods to everyone. When the crowds of the city saw this, they too were astounded at the great miracle that had taken place, and they demanded to know from Saint Conon who had committed the robbery. But he did not tell them who they were; he said, "Let those who lost their property take it back, and let it be enough for them that they have recovered it without harm. And release those held without cause, for God's sake." And so it was done: those who had lost their property recovered it without loss, those arrested without cause were released without ill-treatment, and he did not expose those who had committed the robbery, caring for their salvation.

Since the saint's miracles were flourishing in every way, a great multitude of the Isaurian people turned to our Lord Jesus Christ, and confessing their sins they were baptized, having received the beginning of the knowledge of Christ through Saint Conon. He carefully admonished them to be generous to one another and to abstain from greed, and this they did. So great a grace was given to the faithful through the holy man's teaching that their households prospered, while those of the unbelievers dwindled, so that as a result even more were added to our Lord Jesus Christ.

After a long time, he wanted to return to his own house of prayer, which was near his village of Bidana. The people who lived on Mount Ligrammon, a haunt of brigands, were close by and learned that he was there. They were desperate men, full of ignorance of God. They talked it over among themselves and said that his famous name must mean he had a great deal of money: "Let us not delay. Let us hurry against him, and we will come away with great riches." With this in mind they gathered and rushed against him. They took with them a brigand chief named Cottis, who did not want to go with them. Instead he advised them to give up such an attack on the righteous man. He had been present when Conon worked his miracles, at the time when they were about to celebrate the abominable feast of the idols, and he had seen the idols destroyed and the unclean spirits driven out. So he said to them, "Stop, and do not lay hands on the righteous man." But they would not listen in their frenzy. They kept pressing him and dragged him off by sheer force. When they came within about a stade of the house of prayer, at a place called the Spring of Madness, they stopped and considered how they might get at the saint.

The saint was sitting in quiet. He looked intently and saw some of the demons watching him and shrinking back in fear. At his command they came and stood before him. He asked them, "Why have you come?"
They said, "What do you order us to do?" With authority he ordered them not to trouble or harm any human being, and not to suggest anything base or shameful.

They said, "We have been used to these things from the beginning, and we take delight in plotting against people. We have nothing else to do. So if you want us to give these things up, and if you think of something else, order us and we will do it. Only do not drive us away in anger to go into deserts or waterless and unknown places."

He answered them, "Busy yourselves with farming. Look, those fields over there are still undug. Go, dig them, and tend them well." When they heard this they went away in great fear to do what they had been told.

Yet they knew perfectly well what the robbers were planning, because it was through their own working that the robbery had been suggested to the robbers. And these same demons would also be the ones to hand the robbers over to the punishment that awaited them.

The robbers lingered at that place for a long time, urging their leader Cottis to join them in the attack. When they could not persuade him, they left him behind and set out on their plan. Cottis was grieved at their scheme. He went off by himself near the spring. There he fixed his spears in the ground, threw down his sword, and sat down with his head on his knees, mourning for them, because he expected nothing good to come of it for them.

They came up to the saint's dwelling and knocked at the door. Saint Conon thought they were some of the people who came as usual with requests, or some of the sick, so he opened the door to them. When he saw that they were armed, he supposed they had come from a journey and wanted rest. Each of them kept nudging his neighbor and asking where the place might be where they thought he kept his money. While the robbers were busy searching for the money, Saint Conon hurried to refresh them. He set a table, brought wine, and urged and invited them, saying, "Come, children, have something to eat after your toil." When they could not find what they were after, they turned to anger. They seized him and drew their swords, and raising their hands against him they tried to force him to bring them the money, threatening to kill him.

There was great turmoil and frenzy, and the robbers were ready to kill the righteous man. Suddenly a crowd of demons arrived in haste. These were the very demons who had brought this about by their own working, and they came through the venerable martyr Conon, since they were subject to him. Some of them lit the oven in the monastery. Others rushed upon the band of savage robbers, who had their swords raised to kill the righteous man. They pressed on and terrified them so badly that the robbers went numb as if dead and let their swords drop. Then, lining them up one or two at a time, the demons dragged them off to the fire of the oven. They held their heads to it and scorched them until they were half dead.

Saint Conon took pity on them and ordered the demons to stop, and they stopped. Seeing that the robbers were fainting, he prayed for them, and they revived. When they came to their senses, they got up and fell at his feet, repenting of their boldness. They wept in agony from the pain of the burns, and lying at his feet they begged to be relieved of their great pain. He prayed over them, freed them from pain, and sent them away unharmed. Once released, they ran off as if the fire were still chasing them, until they reached the well at the spring. There they found their leader Cottis in the place where they had left him. He looked hard at them and was amazed to see them still alive. Overjoyed at this unexpected sight, he got up and embraced them. When they told him about the power that had come upon them, he rebuked them for not listening to him from the start. Then they got up and went to their homes, and they told everyone all that had happened to them, so that great fear fell on all who heard it.

Even to this day the fear of Saint Conon remains throughout all that region, and anyone who despises his name soon receives punishment. His name is so venerable, through the grace given him by the Holy Spirit, that once two very wicked Isaurians, who lurked in the mountains with fearsome faces and wild hair, despised his name and disregarded the fear of him. At once the demons came upon them as men who had broken his commands. They seized them by the hair, dragged them along, and carried them, howling and bound, to the feet of the servant of God. The demons wanted to show the people of the neighborhood his holiness more convincingly, and also to increase his authority over the unclean spirits, so much so that at his command they even took charge of farming and tended all kinds of plants and crops.

Among these, at his command, they had a field sown with chickpeas. When the chickpeas were ripe for eating, a traveler came by who did not know the reason for the field. He saw it so flourishing and the crop so abundant and plump that he wanted some. He gave in and took a modest amount. Then, seeing that the field was unguarded, he bent down and cut more without suspecting anything. As he went on gathering handfuls, he heard a voice saying, "That is enough for you; move on." He looked up and around but saw no one, and he went on plucking even more greedily, meaning to load his pack animal.

The voice kept crying out, "Be content; do not be greedy." Again he looked up to see who was shouting, and again he saw no one, but he kept on in his greed. When he had finally taken his fill, he tied it into a bundle to put on his animal. He could barely lift it, and with great effort he hoisted it onto his shoulders.

As he was carrying it and about to put it on his animal as a load, the demon who had been calling out to him at once climbed onto the bundle so that he could not throw it off. It weighed him down and beat him. It sat on his shoulders and drove him along, bringing him to the feet of Saint Conon crushed and sweating from the weight and the lashes of the whips. Bringing him bound to Saint Conon with the chickpeas he had stolen, it accused him: "See, servant of God, we are not as much to blame as wicked and disobedient people. We did what you ordered just now: we dug fields and sowed chickpeas. When they were ripe, as you see, this glutton came along the road, despised the fear of you, and with his greedy heart pulled them up by the handful. I shouted at him loudly and told him many times, 'That is enough, man, what are you doing?' But he did not stop. He despised me too and kept on in his greed, and he ruined our crop, stealing this much all by himself. Now what do you command?"

The servant of Christ saw the man in distress and battered by the evils that had befallen him, and he had compassion on him. First he permitted the unclean spirit to leave and see to its work, and sent it away. It went off sullen because it had not gotten revenge on the thief. Then he rebuked the thief for his boundless greed and urged him never again to attempt such thefts or to be carried away by greed, but to be content with what he had. Then he let him go.

This is still observed in that region to this day. If anyone tries to steal from the enclosures and vineyards that belong to him, whether fruit from the trees, or even leaves, or any of the crops, in any way whatsoever, he cannot escape being whipped at once. Only if he then, with much prayer and confession, brings gold or silver equal in value to what he took will such a person be freed from the torment.

It is the same with the birds at the most holy martyr's shrine, which are countless, and with the herds offered at his holy and glorious annual commemoration: herds of all kinds of cattle and mares, of goats, and many tens of thousands of sheep of various kinds, grazing in the fields and mountains of the Taurus. They are, so to speak, guarded without guards by the fear of him, so that no one dares to try to steal them, or even to touch them at all, since it is dangerous. For if the wrongdoers see only this, the name of his ownership, that is, his sign, which is a tag hung around the neck, they recognize it at once and keep their distance. Not only that, but the shrine's pack animals bear the same sign, so that no one can fail to know them. And all the many possessions belonging to the most holy shrine always remain unmolested through the venerable name of Saint Conon. So greatly did God honor his way of life that even after his death God bore witness to him in these things and made him still more glorious.

Here is yet another miracle besides those already told. A poor widow had an only son, still nursing, whom she carried in her arms as she went begging. At harvest time she went into a glen to gather ears of grain for food, and she set her son down on the ground. While she went over to the reapers and was busy gathering the ears, a huge wolf suddenly appeared, found the child lying there with no one near him, snatched him, and made off. The reapers heard the baby crying, and the mother noticed and turned around. When she realized the disaster was hers, she wailed louder than all of them. Some of the workers shouted, others ran after the beast, but they could not catch it and came back. The mother did not stop to rest. Spreading out her trembling hands, she ran wailing all the way to the holy man to tell him of her calamity, and others went with her.

When they reached the monastery, the child's mother cried out loudly, "Saint Conon, give me my son!" Hearing the sound of lamentation, he hurried out to the door as he usually did. When she saw him, she fell at his feet, clung to him, and wept bitterly. He raised her up and asked what had happened. She was too faint to speak, so those who had come with her told him. When he learned what had happened, he shared the mother's grief. Standing before them all, he lifted his eyes and hands to heaven and prayed. Then, calling on the name of the Holy Trinity, he commanded the demons to go and bring back the beast with the child safe and sound.

Summoned in this way, and unseen, they went off swiftly. They caught up with the wolf a great distance away, still holding the baby in its mouth. Some seized it by the ears and pulled, others pushed from behind, and others beat it, and so they brought the wolf to the feet of Saint Conon. It fell down and laid the child before them all. Everyone cried out and leapt with shouts of joy, and weeping for great joy they glorified God for such power granted to him. He took the child from the mouth of the evil beast and gave him back to his mother. Then, after praying, he dismissed them all, the wolf included.

The great multitude of unclean spirits, driven away from the savor of the idols' sacrifices, was ravaging the region with pestilence. But by the power granted him by the Holy Spirit he banished some of them beyond the borders of the region. Those that roamed about harming people he rebuked; he sternly commanded them in the spirit, made them stand before him, and bound them in the name of Jesus Christ. He took them in thirty earthen jars, secured them, tied them shut, sealed them with lead, and buried them in his own house, as later events have confirmed to us.
These are a few of his many wonders and healings that we have recorded, by which his name was magnified and the report of the achievements of his life spread abroad.

As his fame spread widely, a certain governor named Magnus arrived at the city of Iconium, full of rage. He held authority under an imperial rescript, with orders exceedingly full of threats and murder against the Christians: that if they did not deny the name of Christ, they were to be put to death. When he arrived, he began to rave and say, "If you know of anyone in this city or in the other cities who is a Christian or is called a Christian, report them."

Seeing that he was breathing rage, they told him in fear, "We hear that there is a man in the upper parts of the Taurus called Conon, who belongs to that religion. They say great miracles are done by him, which astonish us all."

He said, "Tell me where he lives, whether in a city or a village, and its name, and how many milestones away it is." They said, "The estate is called Bidana, and it is about forty miles away. We also hear of another man of the same religion named Nisius in the village of Sorobos, on the same road, about twenty miles away."

When he learned this, he gave his orders, set out for the place, and arrived at Sorobos. He stayed there and immediately arrested Saint Nisius and ordered him to be kept under guard. At once he quietly sent for Saint Conon as well from Bidana, as though on some other business, so that no disturbance would arise on his account in that area. For he feared that area, having learned that the people there were bolder and more warlike. The next day Magnus took his seat and ordered Saint Nisius to be brought quickly. His plan was either to persuade him to deny the name of the Lord or to punish him before Saint Conon was brought.

When Saint Nisius was brought before him, he began to ask, "What is your name, and what is your status?" as magistrates customarily do, and all the other questions in order. When he had learned everything from him, and Nisius affirmed, "I am a Christian," he ordered him to be beaten, and roared at him during the beating. Then, easing off, he tried to coax him into denying Christ and joining in his impiety. But Saint Nisius held firm and affirmed the good confession of Christ. He was gentle and guileless, a local man and unschooled in speech, and he used no fine words, for he knew none. But he was noble in faith and endurance, and he gave no other answer than "I am a Christian." Magnus raged all the more, as though determined to defeat him, and ordered harsher tortures to be applied, so that he would die under them before Saint Conon arrived. The torturers beat him without letting up, and he, under the blows, remained silent for many hours in these torments and gave up his soul. Thus nobly and holily Saint Nisius completed his confession of Christ at Sorobos, his own village.

The governor Magnus had been eager to take up this office for no other reason than to destroy the Christians. So after sending to Bidana to summon Saint Conon by a trick, he stayed in Sorobos for no other purpose than to kill Saint Nisius, and that is what he did. Then he got horses and riders ready and hurried swiftly to Bidana, where Saint Conon lived. On the road he overtook the men he had sent ahead, and that same night he entered the village with them before daybreak. He arrested Conon secretly, and without even resting from the journey, he at once took his seat on the tribunal and ordered him to be brought in.

When everyone had gathered for the governor's hearing, they saw Saint Conon being made ready by the governor's attendants, and they were deeply troubled and wept, though they dared say nothing. For they saw his hair, white as wool; he was tall and well proportioned in stature, with stern eyes and a face that was gracious in old age, lacking nothing of the beauty fitting for an elder. When he was brought before the governor, the bystanders raised a great lament over him. The governor, wishing to terrify him, ordered the instruments of torture to be set out before him, and began to address him with flattering and deceitful words: "Seeing that you are an old man, adorned with such gray hair, I take it that your mind is worthy of your appearance. So show wisdom to match your gray hair: renounce and deny this name of Christ, a name of deceit and folly that has turned up among you from I know not where. Then, through me, you will be a friend of the Emperor and of all who hold power. From them every fine thing will be granted you, and whatever is dear to you and to your liking will be yours. And, above all, the priesthood of the greatest gods will be given you, as befitting no one more than your most beautiful and admirable gray hair. And I know that you will love me too, since I will be the one who brings you not only these things but others as well. So if my words and promises please you, give your nod and agree without shame; cast off this nakedness and put on dignity. Do not be minded to oppose me stubbornly as Nisius did, since you see what is set before you, and you will meet the same fate as the one who went before you."

The servant of Christ was unlettered and untrained in the Greek language, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit flowing into him he answered in clear words in the Isaurian language, saying: "You came here riding at full speed, wearing out yourself and those who serve you, so that you might seize me, strip me of my garment, batter me with promises, threats and deceptions, and trick me however you can, or frighten me into denying Christ. You do not know that no one can separate us from the love of Christ: not flattery, not the threat of death, not fire, not the sword. Why do I mention these things you have set before me? You even offer to exchange the things of Christ for the things of demons. You thought you would make a great fool of me, but you yourself have been made a great fool."

Enraged at this, Magnus ordered him to be tortured for many hours. Then he ordered them to let up, and cried out in fury: "You speak to me boldly and profess to philosophize through the [?] of your words, thinking that by such words you will escape the punishment hanging over you? Will you now at least stop this foolish and ill-timed boldness of the Christians, and agree with me, or not? Tell me briefly."

The saint answered and began to speak, to Magnus's shame: "You godless man, more savage than any wild beast! How long will you despise the patience of God and speak against God, setting up falsely named gods against him? They are the works of human hands, made of stone and wood, without movement, and you set them up in opposition to Christ who made all things. You rebel against Christ and enemy of the truth, you have come upon his servants like a wolf and are eager to slaughter them; just as you killed Saint Nisius, you are bent on doing away with me by the same tortures. What wrong have we done that you punish us like this, and persist in torturing us and forcing us to depart from the living God, promising the friendship of the emperor, patronage, gifts of money, and a polluted priesthood? Do you offer me these in exchange for the gifts of God? But this promise of yours will do you no good. Even if you strip off this garment I wear, you will never be able to strip off Christ, whom I have put on. For we have Christ, and we know one God, who is able to rescue us his servants from your hands and from the schemes of your godlessness. For the rest, do what you mean to do."

When the governor heard this he was furious, and ordered him to be thrown down and stretched out with cords, and commanded that he be beaten. Meanwhile he was thinking again about what harsher punishments he might devise and kill him by them.

While he was pondering this and Conon was being beaten, the people of the Isaurian metropolis heard that the governor was punishing Saint Conon at Bidana. Great crowds quickly gathered, armed, and rushed against him. The governor perceived the uproar of the multitude and that they had come against him to help Saint Conon. He had foreseen that this would happen and had saddled horses made ready beforehand; finding them ready, he mounted, took flight, reached Iconium, and found safety there. Some of the Isaurians pursued the governor to seize and kill him, but not catching him they turned back. Most of the crowd went into the building where the governor had been examining the servant of Christ, and found the saint lying stretched out on the ground alone, since all the officials had also scattered in flight. The people of the city untied him and saw his blood streaming from him, and they wailed, weeping and lamenting and pressing against one another. Each of them caught some of the righteous man's flowing blood, wiped it off and smeared it over his own body, believing he would be sanctified by it. Then they carried him off to his own monastery, and took great pains to give him every care and to treat his wounds. When through their care and faith they had restored him to health, each of them took his leave by kissing the righteous man's knees, and so they went home rejoicing.

After this contest and the martyr's faith in Christ that he had displayed, he lived on for two years and completed the course of his life in a good and glorious old age. Those who were present sent word of the saint's falling asleep throughout all that region, and on learning it people came running together as if at a great calamity. The crowd that gathered was beyond counting, and all wept and mourned bitterly as they carried him out, for he had been their guide to the light of true religion and their teacher. They laid him in a coffin where his blessed mother and his blessed betrothed, who had remained ever a virgin, were laid to rest.

After his holy and glorious departure from this life, his dwelling was dedicated as a church. When the foundations were being dug, under the bishop of that time, of holy memory, the diggers came upon the earthenware jars. Seeing that they were sealed with great security and bore lead seals, thirty in number, they were astonished and wondered what they might be. They wanted to lift some of them but could not, since they were extremely heavy and immovable. Delighted by the weight of the jars, they mistakenly supposed they were full of gold and other things, and they broke one of them open. Suddenly they saw two terrible whirlwinds leap out of that jar. These threw all the bystanders to the ground at once and made the air gloomy and dark, so that the builders' winches and all the ropes were torn away on every side, the very frame [?] of the hoist was smashed to the ground, and the building itself was thrown down. Showing themselves to everyone in the air, they cried out, announcing their names. One said, "I am Diomedes"; the other, "I am Cuttonius." As a result such fear and terror fell upon the village that no one any longer dared to be found outside his house after sunset, or to open his door. At the river bridge they threw some people down and drowned them, and they stopped those who wanted to cross, so that the bridge became impassable. The other earthenware jars were put back in that same place, and they remain undisturbed to this day.

But someone will say: "Why did the demons break the bounds he had set them?" Because the people too broke the commands he had constantly urged on everyone, not to be greedy or lovers of money, for he knew that all the evil spirits are the cause of these evils. He had shut them up in the jars, and they remained in subjection to Saint Conon as long as the people kept his commands. But when the people broke the commands, the demons also broke their subjection. When these things had happened, the monks and Christians of the surrounding area came together and kept watch at this bridge with fasting and prayer for some days, and with difficulty they subdued the frenzy of the escaped demons.

We have recalled these few things out of many. As for the healings that took place during his life and are still being performed after his death, no one will be able to recount them all, since our Lord Jesus Christ bears witness to him that these things happen for his glory. For to Christ himself, our God, belongs the glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
